subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which geological time period covers roughly the last 2.6 million years and is studied for evidence of climate change?
questions.explain: The Quaternary period spans approximately the last 2.6 million years and provides much of the evidence for natural climate change.

questions.q: What do scientists analyse in ice cores to work out past atmospheric conditions?
questions.explain: Air bubbles trapped in ice cores preserve samples of the past atmosphere, revealing former greenhouse gas concentrations.

questions.q: In dendrochronology (tree-ring analysis), what does a wide tree ring generally indicate about the year it grew?
questions.explain: Trees grow more in warmer, wetter years, producing wider rings that act as a record of past climate.

questions.q: Why is preserved pollen useful as evidence of past climate?
options: Different plant species thrive in different climates, so pollen shows past conditions
Pollen contains trapped carbon dioxide gas
Pollen colour changes with temperature each year
Pollen records the exact sea level of the past
questions.explain: Identifying pollen preserved in sediment reveals which plants grew there, indicating the climate at the time.

questions.q: A geographer compares two photographs of the same Alpine glacier taken in 1900 and today, showing the ice has retreated far up the valley. This is best used as evidence of what?
questions.explain: Retreating glaciers are a widely used piece of evidence for recent warming of the climate.

questions.q: The Milankovitch cycles describe changes in the Earth's orbit and axis. Which set correctly names the three cycles?
questions.explain: The three Milankovitch cycles are eccentricity (orbit shape), axial tilt (obliquity) and precession (wobble).

questions.q: What does the Milankovitch cycle of 'eccentricity' refer to?
options: Changes in the shape of the Earth's orbit around the Sun
Changes in the angle of the Earth's axis
The wobble of the Earth as it spins
Variations in the number of sunspots
questions.explain: Eccentricity describes how the Earth's orbit shifts between more circular and more elliptical over about 100,000 years.

questions.q: Over roughly what period does the Earth's axial tilt (obliquity) vary in the Milankovitch cycles?
questions.explain: The tilt of the Earth's axis changes over a cycle of approximately 41,000 years.

questions.q: How can variations in solar output (such as sunspot activity) affect the Earth's climate?
options: More solar energy reaching Earth can warm the climate
They add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere
They cause the Earth's orbit to change shape
They release methane from the oceans
questions.explain: Periods of greater solar output deliver more energy to Earth, which can raise temperatures.

questions.q: How can a large volcanic eruption cause short-term cooling of the climate?
options: Ash and gases block incoming sunlight
It releases large amounts of oxygen
It increases the Earth's axial tilt
questions.explain: Volcanic ash and sulphur gases reflect and block sunlight, reducing temperatures for months or years.

questions.q: Which human activity is the main source of the extra carbon dioxide added to the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Burning coal, oil and gas for energy and transport releases large quantities of carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'enhanced greenhouse effect'?
options: Extra greenhouse gases trap more heat, raising global temperatures
The Sun produces more sunspots than usual
questions.explain: Human-added greenhouse gases strengthen the natural greenhouse effect, trapping more heat in the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which of these is a major human source of the greenhouse gas methane?
questions.explain: Cattle digestion and flooded rice fields are significant human sources of methane emissions.

questions.q: A region clears large areas of rainforest for cattle ranching. Why does this contribute to climate change?
options: Fewer trees remove less carbon dioxide from the atmosphere
It cools the local climate permanently
questions.explain: Deforestation removes carbon sinks, so less CO2 is absorbed and more remains in the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which process, driven by warming, directly raises global sea levels even without ice melting?
questions.explain: As seawater warms it expands in volume, raising sea levels alongside the melting of land-based ice.

questions.q: Why are low-lying island nations such as the Maldives especially vulnerable to climate change?
options: Rising sea levels threaten to flood their land
They have no access to fresh water sources at all
questions.explain: Low elevation means even a small rise in sea level can flood large areas and displace communities.

questions.q: In responses to climate change, what does 'mitigation' mean?
options: Reducing the causes, for example cutting greenhouse gas emissions
Coping with the effects once they happen
questions.explain: Mitigation tackles the causes of climate change, mainly by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of adaptation rather than mitigation?
options: Building higher sea walls to cope with rising sea levels
Switching power stations to solar energy
Planting new forests to absorb carbon
questions.explain: Adaptation means adjusting to the effects of climate change, such as defending coasts, rather than reducing its causes.

questions.q: A low-lying coastal city expects more frequent storm surges as the climate warms. Which is an adaptation response?
options: Improving flood defences and warning systems
Closing all its coal power stations
questions.explain: Strengthening defences and warnings helps the city cope with impacts, which is adaptation.

questions.q: A government wants to mitigate climate change by cutting emissions. Which policy best achieves this?
options: Increasing electricity generation from renewable sources
Relocating villages away from the coast
questions.explain: Using renewables reduces greenhouse gas emissions, addressing the causes of climate change (mitigation).
